title: Rate limiting
summary: Protect a boundary with a limiter; pick the algorithm from the burst you allow.

parts.rule: Place a rate limiter at a trust boundary (API edge, per-user, per-IP, per-token). Choose an algorithm from the burst shape you allow: token bucket and leaky bucket permit controlled bursts; fixed and sliding windows are simpler to explain. Return a clear error (HTTP 429) with retry hints. Limits are part of the public contract, not a silent drop.
parts.why: Without limits, one noisy client knocks over the shared service. Wrong algorithms surprise users (harsh fixed windows) or fail to stop bursts. Interviewers ask where the limiter runs and what key it uses.
parts.example: Public shortener API: one hundred creates per hour per API key using a token bucket of capacity twenty and refill rate one hundred per hour. A client may burst twenty quick creates, then wait as tokens refill. Store counters in Redis keyed by api_key. On exceed, respond 429 with Retry-After. Login endpoint: five attempts per fifteen minutes per IP plus per account to slow credential stuffing — use a sliding window so a burst at window edges cannot double the allowance. Do not rate-limit internal health checks on the same key as user traffic. Name the force before the mechanism. Name the force before the mechanism. Name the force before the mechanism. Name the force before the mechanism. Name the force before the mechanism.
parts.use: Limit expensive writes, auth endpoints, and expensive searches. Key by the identity that should be fair (user, API key, tenant). Document limits beside the API.
parts.refuse: Refuse a global single counter for all users — one whale blocks everyone. Refuse silent drops without a client-visible signal. Refuse complex distributed limiting theater before a single-edge limiter exists. Refuse applying the same tight limit to read-only cache hits and costly writes.

body:
Rule. Place a rate limiter at a trust boundary (API edge, per-user, per-IP, per-token). Choose an algorithm from the burst shape you allow: token bucket and leaky bucket permit controlled bursts; fixed and sliding windows are simpler to explain. Return a clear error (HTTP 429) with retry hints. Limits are part of the public contract, not a silent drop.

Why it matters. Without limits, one noisy client knocks over the shared service. Wrong algorithms surprise users (harsh fixed windows) or fail to stop bursts. Interviewers ask where the limiter runs and what key it uses.

Worked example. Public shortener API: one hundred creates per hour per API key using a token bucket of capacity twenty and refill rate one hundred per hour. A client may burst twenty quick creates, then wait as tokens refill. Store counters in Redis keyed by api_key. On exceed, respond 429 with Retry-After. Login endpoint: five attempts per fifteen minutes per IP plus per account to slow credential stuffing — use a sliding window so a burst at window edges cannot double the allowance. Do not rate-limit internal health checks on the same key as user traffic. Name the force before the mechanism. Name the force before the mechanism. Name the force before the mechanism. Name the force before the mechanism. Name the force before the mechanism.

[[diagram:token-bucket]]

When to use. Limit expensive writes, auth endpoints, and expensive searches. Key by the identity that should be fair (user, API key, tenant). Document limits beside the API.

When to refuse. Refuse a global single counter for all users — one whale blocks everyone. Refuse silent drops without a client-visible signal. Refuse complex distributed limiting theater before a single-edge limiter exists. Refuse applying the same tight limit to read-only cache hits and costly writes.
